chunks: "The big picture is that GPUs specialize for a workload where there are millions of independent, similar pieces of work, and every optimization exploits that.
First, massive parallelism and SIMT: instead of a complex front end per thread, one fetch and decode feeds 32 lanes, so the overhead per operation is tiny.
Second, latency hiding by multithreading: tens of thousands of threads and a huge register file mean no need for big caches or speculation.
Third, very high memory bandwidth, with wide GDDR or HBM buses, plus texture caches and compression of color, depth and textures to cut traffic.
Fourth, fixed-function hardware for rasterization, texture filtering and blending, which is much more energy-efficient than doing it in shaders.
And they run at lower clock and voltage, which gives much better energy per operation. The trade-offs follow directly. Single-thread performance is poor.
Branch divergence and uncoalesced memory accesses waste lanes and bandwidth. You need huge amounts of parallel work to hit peak.
The big register file and wide memory interface cost area and power, and memory capacity is limited compared with system RAM.
Fixed-function blocks are inflexible if the workload changes. And programming is harder, because you have to think about warps, memory patterns and occupancy."
